title: NBA League Pass Rankings: Part I
subtitle: An annual tradition finds a new home. Let the countdown begin.
contentHtml:
What better way to launch the Lowe Post newsletter than by unveiling our 13th-annual NBA League Pass rankings—which really should be our 15th edition, but we digress.

If you’re new here—hello, and thank you for checking this out!—these rankings measure watchability. They are not power rankings. Teams can rank anywhere here (almost) regardless of win-loss quality. This is about sheer entertainment value.

As we have done since the first #LPRs in the halcyon Grantland days, we rank teams on a scale of 1-10 in five categories:

  • Zeitgeist: Do regular people want to talk about this team? Is it on what now comprises national “television”?

  • Highlights and stars: Are there players who could at any moment erupt into transcendence?

  • Style: This category judges the executives who build rosters and the coaches who direct them: Is this team fun to watch? Does it play with variety?

  • League Pass minutiae: I live with all these teams every night for many, many months. Their jerseys, courts, and announcers burrow into my five senses and never leave. Are they additive or annoying?

  • Unintentional comedy: This category is the fault of both Bill Simmons and the JaVale McGee–Andray Blatche–Nick Young–Ted Leonsis–blogging–crazy–stuff Washington Wizards.

I add up scores from all five categories to arrive at one composite score for each team. We reveal them here in reverse order—starting with no. 30.

I am a prisoner of the sacred #LPR algorithm. If you are mad about your team’s placement, you are mad at math.

A quick programming note before we dive into it: We will publish these rankings in five parts between now and opening night. This first part is available for free; Parts 2 through 5 will be for paid subscribers only. Once the season tips off, The Lowe Post will convert to its normal weekly cadence.

30. Milwaukee Bucks (19.5)

Every year, one unlucky team ends up in the basement, and my reaction is always the same: “Wow! I’m sort of excited to watch them!” On the court, the league is in a good place. (Off the court, it is awash in scandal and billions of somewhat unknown origins. Good times!)

The Giannis Antetokounmpo trade left in its wake A Bunch of Guys—a gaggle of strangers waiting in an airport terminal for flights to somewhere else. There are a gazillion guards and wings who need the ball, stealing minutes and touches from the real League Pass headliners: Kasparas Jakucionis, throwing Diet Luka blind overhead passes; Brayden Burries, a burly jack-of-all-trades who may well be the steal of the draft; the gangly Ousmane Dieng, a sneaky Most Improved Player candidate looking to build on his late-season breakout; and Jaime Jaquez Jr., my pick last season for Sixth Man of the Year, a whirling dervish of flopping hair and old-school banked-in flip shots.

Will they all be feeding Gary “The $16 Million Man” Trent Jr.? Will the broadcast team even acknowledge Trent’s hilarious contract? (Marques Johnson is a star analyst on the Bucks broadcast, but give Wesley Matthews a listen when he gets reps; he’s really good, with huge potential. National networks should pay attention.)

Jericho Sims can eat the rim. Nate Ament is … something? Will Kyle Kuzma focus more on off-ball defense or exchanging crypto investment tips with the courtside glitterati?

The other major attraction is Kel’el Ware, one of the centerpieces in the Antetokounmpo return. The Bucks should let him explore all parts of his inside-outside arsenal now that Ware is 1,500 miles from Erik Spoelstra’s doghouse. There is maybe a 25 percent chance Ware makes an All-Star team someday if he amps up his work habits and harnesses each of his talents in the right dose. He and Myles Turner should be able to toggle inside-outside roles on both ends when Taylor Jenkins pairs them.

The art is fine; dark green is my favorite color, though the Bucks’ version is blander than I’d prefer. Jenkins will instill order. He will set a base identity on both ends and have this hodgepodge at least executing a few core precepts.

29. Los Angeles Clippers (21)

This is going to be brutal. The only reason the Boingo Tree Planters aren’t last is Darius Garland, a maestro of hesitation moves, eye fakes, hook passes, and floaters launched on the way up—all the ploys little guys have to master. It’s rare to look so smooth while playing with a staccato rhythm.

The semimonthly Brandon Ingram midrange heater is worth an #LPR point or two. Wait, doctors discovered that Ingram had a partially torn Achilles during heel surgery? Max Strus is hurt too? My God, the Clippers.

Give me all the Yanic Konan Niederhauser minutes. Keaton Wagler brings intrigue, even if he’s likely to come off the bench until the Clippers trade all the veterans here biding time until their escape.

Derrick Jones Jr. works only on a good team, and he doesn’t dunk enough for his Airplane Mode highlights to bump L.A.’s score much. Kris Dunn damn near makes opposing ball handlers quit with his in-your-jersey defense. What is Bradley Beal even doing here?

But … man. Dead crowds. No Steve Ballmer churning his piston arms like a nerd who just found out about the release of another Avengers movie. The broadcast is so-so, though Mike Fratello and Jim Jackson are aces. The art is … fine. Even the Gradey Dick jokes are played out. Wait! Jordan Miller is only 26, and he has a nice combination of physicality and skill! He might be a building block! What? He’s injured already? Pathos is not comedy.

Should everyone involved just concede defeat and either contract the Clippers or move them literally anywhere else? What a disaster.

28. Brooklyn Nets (22.5)

The Kings outrank Brooklyn only because of Sacramento’s stranglehold on the unintentional comedy category. The algorithm also gave Brooklyn the lowest zeitgeist score since the New York Knicks’ championship officially banished the Nets to afterthought status in their own metropolitan area; they lost any chance at an entire generation of fans.

The minimalist art is pristine, with flourishes new and old—including the return (again) of the Notorious B.I.G.–inspired “Coogi” alternate jerseys. Am I taking partial credit—stemming from my 2016 oral history—for the Nets finally holding Swamp Dragons Night, complete with appropriately garish and lizardy merchandise? Yes. Yes, I am. I will be there, and I will be buying everything.

The broadcast team has become overcrowded, but only because some mainstays—namely, Ian Eagle and Sarah Kustok—have too many other assignments to turn their lives over to this sad-sack franchise.

Oh, the team? It’ll be fun! Jordi Fernandez always has these guys applying pressure on defense and taking the right kinds of shots. The Egor Demin–Mikel Brown Jr. tandem could be a long-term pillar. They should complement each other, Brown the slicing scorer, Demin the chameleon whose combination of size, shooting, passing, and defense fits alongside anyone. (He just needs to remember that you are indeed allowed to dribble into that painted rectangle near the basket.)

Day’Ron Sharpe is a rebound muncher who is finally getting his chance. Mo Wagner will draw a charge and let the entire arena hear about it. He is one the league’s great agitators; there is always a chance of an altercation when Wagner is on the floor.

Danny Wolf passes like an NBA game is one continuous dare: Oh, you don’t think I can throw this 50-foot lefty bounce pass between three defenders, through the last one’s legs, and right on target to Michael Porter Jr.? Watch me. His passes might smack an unsuspecting teammate in the head. Every seat in the first five rows should come with a warning placard: Please put down your phones when Danny Wolf is in the game.

Remember when Terance Mann held up the James Harden trade? What a time.

Also, Julius Randle is here. Just a reminder.

27. Sacramento Kings (23.5)

Until this woebegone franchise sniffs competency, the unintentional comedy category gives it a floor of no. 29 on this list. Which pseudo-celebrity is Vivek Ranadive cozying up to courtside tonight? Or is it yet another member of the Kings’ 2002 conference finals team—maybe Lawrence Funderburke was in town? (I loved that dude.)

Are any fans wearing paper bags?

Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis are the NBA incarnation of that internet girl who weeps through her dance routine: professionals who won’t be able to hide the creeping existential despair. LaVine doesn’t dunk much anymore, neutering the team’s score in the highlight category.

And a reminder: Doug Christie committed a coaching error so egregious—intentionally fouling Seth Curry in crunch time, with the Warriors in the bonus—that fans accused him of tanking a game, only for the Kings’ public defense to be We’re not tanking. We’re just that dumb. If you tried to explain to a non–NBA fan everything that has gone wrong for Sacramento in the past 20 years—botched picks, on-court lowlights, inexplicable trades, firing any coach who begins to right the ship—they would not believe all of it could have befallen one franchise.

Dylan Cardwell’s rim-rattling enthusiasm moves Sacramento up another spot or two. Cardwell is a third-string center who has taken it upon himself to cleanse the vibes. He’ll slam a putback that cuts the Kings’ deficit to 18, look to the crowd, smile wide, and implore them to cheer. Some fans respond. Others look confused: Wait, is this player actually this enthused about Kings basketball?

Ben Simmons looks healthier and more explosive, and I am genuinely rooting for a renaissance—even if his aversion to getting fouled defangs his offensive game. There is some unintentional comedy in watching Simmons veer toward the sideline the minute he crosses half court. Those bouts of fear have subsided, at least in the preseason.

The real draw is the quartet of Darius Acuff Jr., Nique Clifford, Maxime Raynaud, and Keegan Murray. The Kings need to find at least two long-term starters from this bunch, even if one—maybe Murray, pending a bounce-back—is a fifth-starter/3-and-D role player type. Raynaud, who should have made first-team All-Rookie last season, is, of course, already injured. #KANGZ

Acuff will get the keys right away. He won’t be efficient as a rookie, but there is real promise in his manipulative bob-and-weave chemistry with two very talented—and very different—screeners in Sabonis and Raynaud. Acuff moves like a pro.

Raynaud thrives where others don’t venture; more than half of his attempts came from floater range last season, and he hit a Jokic-ian 55 percent of those buttery shots. Can he defend well enough to start? Raynaud played spot minutes next to Sabonis last season in an extra-large lineup; why not get crazy and go super-big? Precious Achiuwa will play decent minutes too.

Clifford is jitterbug clever, all jagged, arrhythmic dribbles and hesitation fakes. He can shoot, pass, and read the floor. Start him and feed him all he can handle.

26. Washington Wizards (25)

The algorithm must be scarred from the hideous tanktastic basketball Washington played last season, including in a home arena so empty that courtside mics picked up every raspy plea from head coach Brian Keefe—arms flapping, wide-eyed with desperate, hopeless confusion.

It does not help Washington’s score that Chris Miller’s rapturous play-by-play chronicles any semi-functional Wizards action as if it were a Michelangelo brushstroke in the Sistine Chapel. (Drew Gooden, the Wiz analyst, has a harder time hiding his displeasure.)

Alas, the algorithm cannot reward the Wiz for Bub Carrington’s honesty about Washington’s goals for the entirety of his career. He said the quiet part out loud. I would have paid real money to attend the urgent public relations info session that followed Carrington telling the truth: Just say we tried our best. Use the word “culture” a lot!

But this is a new season! Trae Young and Anthony Davis bring All-Star pedigree and up-the-middle structure on both ends—presuming they play, and that Davis, without an extension, does not pout. Young is one of the best little-guy passers ever, with every dish in his bag—lobs from all angles and ambidextrous crosscourt frozen ropes that are usually reserved for taller ball handlers.

The Davis–Alex Sarr fit will be fascinating. Sarr is quicker, but are there nights when it will make sense to have him guard opposing centers—stashing Davis in something like a one-man zone? Could Keefe try a full-on zone? How will they split traditional interior roles on offense?

AJ Dybantsa is ready to cook, but he’ll have to learn life away from the ball alongside Young and Davis. The other exciting young guys slot into roles more befitting their talent levels: well-rounded Kyshawn George, slippery Will Riley, slick and guileless Tre Johnson.

What is the over/under on the number of days before Deandre Ayton’s first oblivious quote? Who is more surprised to wake up every morning and see Wizards gear strewn around their home, Ayton or Davis?

Young’s logo 3 spasms are like when my kid scarfs cotton candy at the carnival: gluttonous fun in the moment, but on the next ride, it’s clear she’s made a mistake. The combined foul grifting between Young and Dybantsa might be grating.

The art stinks, save for the cherry blossom jerseys. The Wiz, being the Wiz, will probably mothball them for the next decade in favor of blandly patriotic pajamas. (Update: Maybe not! The Wiz seem open to a long-overdue rebrand, according to The Athletic.) Still, for the time being, the overall minutiae score dropped these guys three spots lower than they should be.

This team won’t be bad, or boring. There is a lot to like. The league is just awash in entertaining teams.

25. New Orleans Pelicans (25.5)

I’m going into this Pelicans season the same way I’ll plop into my seat for Digger: I have no idea what the hell this loud mishmash is or what it’s supposed to be, but I won’t be able to resist rubbernecking. (There’s a reason New Orleans headlined my annual “Most Confusing Teams” episode of The Zach Lowe Show.)

How can Jamahl Mosley fashion a cohesive offense around this pile of disparate parts? Dejounte Murray and Jeremiah Fears want the ball to run pick-and-roll; Fears is an imaginative, foundational gunslinger, and Murray looked in his brief return last season like the stabilizer this manic unit so badly needs. Zion Williamson and Bennedict Mathurin want the ball to Kool-Aid Man their way to the basket. Saddiq Bey wants the ball to bully suckers on the wing. Derik Queen—the other young tentpole—wants the ball to run the show from the elbow. Jordan Poole just wants to turn back time to the day before Draymond Green punched him in the face. (He also wants the ball.) Trey Murphy III wants the ball to continue proving he is more than an ace 3-point shooter and hellacious dunker.

Some of these guys also want the ball because they are playing for contracts. Few of them are reliable 3-point shooters. Fewer still are plus defenders.

The roster appears to make no sense, but there will be quarters when the Pelicans are flying and Zion is pogo-sticking for putbacks and Herbert Jones is deflecting everything and Deandre Jordan is cheering and Antonio Daniels is cackling and Queen is decelerating into soft layups (or hitting Zion with lobs)—and you will say to yourself (because you certainly wouldn’t say it aloud to any normal person), Hey, maybe this team makes sense? Did they just score 45 points in 12 minutes?

Then they will give up 40 in the next 12 and lose.
